title: How to get your motorcycle ready for a long trip
alt: A dark green motorcycle loaded with a tail bag and a helmet, parked on a dusty roadside
excerpt: A long ride puts more miles on your bike in a few days than it might see in a month. Here is what to check before you leave, so the trip is about the road and not the hard shoulder.

body.p: A multi-day trip is the best thing you can do on a motorcycle, and also the hardest thing you can ask of it. Hundreds of miles in a few days, extra weight from luggage, unfamiliar roads and no garage nearby. Most trip-ending problems are things that could have been spotted at home with an hour of preparation. A quick look over the bike, done a few days before you leave, also gives you time to order a part if something needs replacing.

body.h: Look at what is due before you go

body.p: Start with the bike's service history. Add the distance of your trip to the current odometer reading and see what that number crosses. If the oil change or a chain and sprocket check is due halfway through the trip, do it before you leave. Finding a workshop in a town you have never visited, on a day you planned to ride, is nobody's idea of a holiday.

ul: Tyres: check the tread depth across the whole width and the age of the tyres. A tyre that would last another month at home may not last two thousand miles.
Pressures: set them for the load you will carry. Your manual usually lists a higher figure for a passenger or luggage.
Chain: clean, lube and adjust it, and look for tight spots and hooked sprocket teeth.
Brakes: check pad thickness and fluid level, and make sure the lever and pedal feel firm.
Fluids and lights: top up the oil and coolant, and check every bulb, including the brake light.

body.p: Luggage changes how a bike handles. Keep heavy items low and close to the centre, and spread weight evenly across panniers. Adjust the rear preload if your suspension allows it, and take a short ride fully loaded before the trip so the first time you feel the difference is not on a mountain pass.

Bring the tool kit that came with the bike, a tyre plug kit with a way to reinflate, a few cable ties, some tape, a spare fuse and a small bottle of chain lube for longer trips. Save your breakdown cover number and a photo of your documents on your phone.

body.h: Keep a record as you ride

body.p: Note the odometer at the start and end of the trip and each day in between. You will know exactly how far you went, and when you get home you will know which services the trip pulled forward. Those miles count just as much as the commute, and they are easy to forget.

MotoLog makes that part simple: log the trip and its mileage, and the app shows which services are due soon or overdue before you set off and when you get back. You can get it in the section just below.

title: The basic toolkit every rider should own
alt: An open socket set in a black case on a concrete garage floor, with a ratchet and loose sockets beside it
excerpt: You don't need a workshop to look after your bike. A small, well-chosen set of tools covers most of the jobs that keep it running well between services.

body.p: Plenty of riders leave every job to the dealer, and that is fine for the big services. But a lot of what keeps a motorcycle healthy is small, regular work: adjusting the chain, checking tyre pressures, topping up fluids, tightening something that has worked loose. With a modest toolkit you can do all of that at home, in less time than it takes to book an appointment.

body.h: Start with what your bike actually uses

body.p: Before you buy anything, look at your bike. Note the sizes of the bolts you touch most often, such as the axle nut, the chain adjusters and the sump plug, and check the owner's manual for the torque figures. Buying the right sizes once is cheaper than a big generic set full of tools you never use.

ul: A socket set with a ratchet, covering the common sizes on your bike, plus a few extensions.
Combination spanners in the same sizes, for places a socket cannot reach.
A set of hex keys, and Torx bits if your bike uses them.
A torque wrench, so axle nuts, sump plugs and brake bolts go back to the right figure.
A good tyre pressure gauge. The one on a petrol station airline is not always accurate.
Chain cleaner, a soft brush and chain lube.
Nitrile gloves, rags and a drain pan for anything involving oil.

body.p: A paddock stand makes chain and wheel work far easier on bikes without a centre stand. A small battery maintenance charger keeps the battery healthy if the bike sits for weeks. A head torch and a magnetic pick-up tool will save your temper the first time a washer drops into the fairing.

body.h: Carry a small kit on the bike

body.p: For trips, a compact roll under the seat is worth its weight: the tool kit that came with the bike, a tyre plug kit with a few CO2 cartridges or a small pump, cable ties, a little tape and a spare fuse or two. It will not fix everything, but it turns plenty of roadside problems into a short stop instead of a recovery call.

body.h: Tools are only half of it

body.p: Doing your own small jobs is satisfying, but it is easy to lose track of what you did and when. Was the chain adjusted last month or last season? When did the oil go in? Writing it down each time, with the date and the odometer reading, gives you a proper service history and tells you when the next job is due. That record is also exactly what a buyer wants to see when you sell.

If you would rather not keep that record in a notebook, MotoLog logs your services and mileage and flags each job as due soon or overdue, so your toolkit comes out at the right time. You can get the app just below.

title: How to store your motorcycle for winter
alt: A black sport motorcycle with a green frame resting on a paddock stand in a dark garage
excerpt: A few hours of preparation in autumn means a bike that starts first time in spring. Here is what to do before you park it up, and what to check when you bring it back.

body.p: When the days get short and the roads turn wet and salty, plenty of riders park the bike until spring. Done carelessly, that break can leave you with a flat battery, stale fuel and tyres with flat spots. Done well, it takes an afternoon and the bike is ready to go the first warm weekend of the year.

Road grime, salt and dead insects keep working on paint, alloy and chrome while the bike is parked. Give it a proper wash, dry it thoroughly, and pay attention to the wheels, the swingarm and the underside of the engine. A coat of wax or a protective spray on bare metal helps too. A clean bike also makes it easier to spot leaks over the winter.

body.h: Change the oil now, not in spring

body.p: Used oil carries acids and contaminants from combustion, and they sit against the inside of the engine for months if you leave them there. Changing the oil and filter before storage means the engine rests in clean oil. If an oil change is close to due anyway, this is the obvious time to do it.

body.h: Look after the fuel and the battery

ul: Fill the tank close to full to reduce condensation, and add a fuel stabiliser if the bike will sit for more than a month or so. Run the engine briefly so treated fuel reaches the fuel system.
Connect the battery to a smart maintenance charger, or remove it and keep it somewhere cool and dry on a charger.
Check your manual for anything specific to your bike, such as draining a carburettor.

body.h: Take the weight off the tyres

body.p: Tyres that sit in one position for months can develop flat spots. Put the bike on a paddock stand or centre stand if you can, so one or both wheels are off the ground. If not, pump the tyres up to the recommended pressure and move the bike a little every few weeks.

body.h: Cover it and keep it dry

body.p: A garage or shed is ideal. Use a breathable cover rather than a plastic sheet, which traps moisture against the bike. If the bike has to stay outside, an outdoor cover that is designed to vent is worth the money. Plugging the exhaust outlets keeps out damp and small animals, as long as you remember to remove the plugs before you start it.

body.h: Write down where you left off

body.p: Before you walk away, record the date and the odometer reading, along with what you did: oil changed, battery on charge, fuel treated. It takes a minute, and in March it answers the question you will otherwise be guessing at. In MotoLog you can log the mileage and the services you did, and because service intervals can be set by time as well as distance, anything that falls due over the winter still shows up as due soon or overdue.

ul: Remove exhaust plugs and the cover, and refit the charged battery.
Check tyre pressures, chain tension and lubrication, and brake fluid level.
Look underneath for leaks and test the brakes before your first proper ride.
Check what services came due while the bike was parked.

body.p: An afternoon of preparation now saves you a dead battery and a frustrating first ride. Park it carefully, write down where you left off, and the bike will be ready when the roads are.

title: How often should you change your motorcycle's oil?
alt: A rider working on a motorcycle in a garage with a socket set laid out beside the bike
excerpt: Oil is the cheapest insurance your engine has. Here is how to work out the right interval for your bike, and how to stop it slipping past.

body.p: Engine oil does more than lubricate. It cools, cleans and protects everything inside the engine, and on most motorcycles it also looks after the clutch and gearbox. Old oil does all of that worse, which is why an oil change is the service most riders will do more often than any other.

body.h: Start with the manual, then adjust for how you ride

body.p: Your owner's manual gives a service interval, usually as a distance, a time, or both, whichever comes first. That second part matters. A bike that only does a few hundred miles a year still needs fresh oil, because oil ages in the sump even when the bike is parked.

Then think about how you actually ride. Short trips that never fully warm the engine, stop-start city riding, hot weather, track days and heavy loads are all harder on oil than steady road miles. If that sounds like you, changing earlier than the maximum is a sensible habit.

ul: The oil on the dipstick or in the sight glass looks very dark or gritty.
The engine feels rougher or noisier than usual.
The gearbox is notchy or the clutch feels different.
You cannot remember when you last changed it.

body.p: That last one is the most common. Most missed services are not a decision to skip them. The date and the mileage just fade from memory.

Change the oil filter at the same time. A fresh filter holds the contaminants that fresh oil picks up, and the manual usually pairs the two. While the bike is on the stand, it is also a good moment to check the sump plug washer and look over the chain and tyres.

The easiest way to stay on schedule is to record each oil change when you do it: the date, the odometer reading and what you used. Then you always know what is coming. In MotoLog you set an interval by distance or time, and the app flags the service as due soon and then overdue, so it never depends on your memory.
Check your manual for the interval that applies to your bike, set it once, and let the reminders do the remembering.

title: Motorcycle chain maintenance: clean, lube and adjust
alt: A hand spraying lubricant onto a motorcycle chain
excerpt: A neglected chain wears out sprockets, costs power and can fail at the worst time. A few minutes of regular care keeps it quiet and safe.

body.p: On a chain-driven motorcycle, the chain is the last link between the engine and the road. It works hard, it is exposed to water and grit, and it tells you when it is unhappy: noise, rough running or a stiff, rusty look.
The good news is that chain care is quick, cheap and easy to do at home. The less good news is that it is also easy to put off.

Grit mixed with old lube forms a grinding paste that wears the chain and the sprockets. Use a chain brush and a cleaner that is safe for your chain type (check for O-ring or X-ring compatibility), wipe it down, and let it dry before you apply anything new.

Apply chain lube to the inside run of the chain while you slowly turn the rear wheel, so it gets thrown outwards and works into the rollers. Do it when the chain is warm from a ride, and let it sit before you head out so it does not fling off onto the wheel.

A chain that is too loose can jump the sprockets. One that is too tight strains the gearbox and wheel bearings. Your manual gives the correct slack measurement. Check it at the tightest point of the chain, because chains do not wear evenly.

Many riders lube roughly every few hundred miles and after riding in the rain, and clean when the chain looks dirty. Manuals vary, so use the interval for your own bike as a guide and adjust for your conditions: dust, salt and wet roads all call for more attention.

ul: Lube: little and often.
Clean: when it is dirty or before a long trip.
Slack check: regularly, and after any adjustment.
Replace the chain and sprockets as a set when they are worn.

body.h: Track it like any other service

body.p: Chain care is a perfect fit for distance-based reminders. In MotoLog you can set up a recurring chain clean and lube, so you see it flagged as due soon before it becomes overdue, and you can log it in a few seconds when it is done.

title: Why you should track your motorcycle's mileage
alt: Close-up of a motorcycle tachometer and instrument cluster
excerpt: Your odometer is more useful than it looks. Logging it regularly makes servicing, budgeting and resale easier.

body.p: Most riders glance at the odometer without thinking much about it. But the number is the backbone of nearly every maintenance decision: when oil is due, when the chain needs attention, when tyres and brake fluid should be looked at. If you do not know your mileage, you cannot know what is due.

Service intervals are usually written in distance, time, or both. Without a recent odometer reading you are guessing how far you are from the next one. A short log of readings, even just after rides, turns that guess into a clear number.

body.h: See how much you really ride

body.p: It is surprisingly common to be wrong about how much you ride. Some riders discover they cover far more than they thought, and need to service more often. Others find the bike sits idle, so time-based intervals matter more than distance. Tracking your distance per month and per year shows which one applies to you.

ul: Plan service and parts costs more accurately.
Spot a change in usage, like a new commute.
Know when a warranty or inspection limit is approaching.
Have an accurate figure ready when you sell.

body.p: You do not need a spreadsheet. Note the odometer at the end of a ride or whenever you fuel up, and let the numbers build up. The habit matters more than the method.
With MotoLog you log your odometer after a ride and see your distance per month and per year. Your service reminders then match how much you actually ride, instead of how much you think you ride.

title: The 5-minute pre-ride check every rider should do
alt: A rider in a black helmet and leathers on a mountain road
excerpt: A quick walk around the bike before you set off catches most problems while they are still small. Here is a simple routine you can repeat every time.

body.p: A motorcycle gives you less margin for error than a car, so a short check before you ride is time well spent. It takes about five minutes once it becomes a habit, and it catches the kind of small problems that turn into big ones at speed.

Check tyre pressures with a gauge when the tyres are cold, and compare them to the figures in your manual. Look at the tread and sidewalls for cuts, bulges or embedded objects. Under-inflated tyres affect handling and wear faster.

Pull the brake and clutch levers and check they move smoothly and return fully. Press the brake pedal. Check that the throttle snaps closed when released. Look for fluid levels in the brake reservoirs and for any leaks around the calipers.
Switch on the ignition and check the headlight, brake light, indicators and horn. A bike that others cannot see or hear is a bike at risk.

ul: Chain: slack and lubrication, as per your manual.
Oil and coolant: levels at the correct marks.
Fuel: enough for the ride, with a margin.
Bolts and bags: nothing loose, luggage secure.

body.h: Make it a habit, then back it up

body.p: The pre-ride check catches what you can see today. The service schedule catches what you cannot: wear that builds up over distance and time. Used together they cover both. MotoLog keeps the second half in order by flagging each service as it comes due, so your walk-around only has to cover the first.
A few minutes before every ride is a small price for arriving where you meant to go.

title: How to plan a motorcycle trip you will actually enjoy
alt: A group of motorcyclists riding on a curving road lined with trees
excerpt: A good ride starts before you leave the driveway. Plan the route, the stops and the bike, and the trip takes care of itself.

body.p: The best motorcycle trips are rarely the most complicated. They are the ones where the route is comfortable, the stops are in the right places and the bike behaves. A little planning is what makes that possible.

body.h: Choose a route that suits the bike and the riders

body.p: Pick a start, a destination and a rough distance you will be happy to cover in a day. Be realistic: curvy roads, weather and photo stops all slow you down. If you ride with others, plan around the least experienced rider, not the fastest.

Know roughly how far your bike goes on a tank, and plan fuel stops with a margin, especially in remote areas. Build in a break every couple of hours. Tired riders make mistakes, and breaks make the ride more enjoyable anyway.

body.h: Check the bike before you go

body.p: Before a long trip, look at the things that matter most: tyres, brakes, oil, chain, lights and coolant. Is a service due soon? It is much better to do it a week before the trip than to find out about it two hundred miles from home.

ul: Check what is due soon or overdue on your bike.
Look over tyres, brakes, fluids and chain.
Pack basic tools, a puncture repair kit and a phone charger.
Tell someone your route and rough timings.

body.h: Keep a record of the trip

body.p: Trips are worth remembering, and the distance counts towards your maintenance. In MotoLog you can map out your next ride with a start, a destination, dates and notes, mark it as ridden afterwards, and the distance goes straight into your log. That keeps your mileage accurate and your service reminders in step with what you really rode.
Plan the practical parts, then leave plenty of room for the unplanned ones. That is where the best stories come from.

title: A simple motorcycle maintenance schedule
alt: A rider working on a motorcycle in a garage with tools laid out beside the bike
excerpt: Oil, chain, tyres, brake fluid and more: what to look at, how often, and how to keep it all straight without a notebook.

body.p: Motorcycles are not complicated to look after, but there are a lot of small jobs, each with its own interval. Some are measured in distance, others in time, and it is easy to lose track of which is next.
Always follow the schedule in your own manual, since it varies by model. As a general guide, these are the areas most riders keep an eye on.

ul: Tyre pressure and condition.
Chain slack and lubrication.
Oil and coolant levels.
Lights, brakes and controls.
Engine oil and filter, by distance or time.
Air filter, inspected and replaced when dirty.
Spark plugs, at the interval your manual gives.
Brake pads, checked for wear.

body.p: Some things age even if the bike barely moves. Brake fluid absorbs moisture over time, and coolant has a service life too. Manuals typically give these in years rather than miles, which is exactly the kind of thing that is easy to forget.

Valve clearances, chain and sprocket replacement, fork oil and tyre replacement come around less often, but they are significant. Having a record of the last time you did each one makes the next decision straightforward.

body.h: One place for all of it

body.p: The hard part is not knowing what to do. It is remembering when. In MotoLog you add each service with an interval by distance or time, and the app shows what is due soon and what is overdue. When you do the job, you log it, and the clock starts again.
Set up your list once, and it keeps working for you every ride after that.

title: How a service history helps your motorcycle sell for more
alt: A dark green café racer motorcycle parked in front of a roller shutter
excerpt: Buyers pay more for a bike they can trust. A clear record of services and mileage is one of the easiest ways to show that.

body.p: When someone buys a used motorcycle, they are buying the previous owner's habits as much as the machine. They cannot see how it was looked after, so they look for evidence.

ul: Regular oil changes with dates and mileage.
Evidence of major services done on time.
A believable odometer history.
Proof that wear items were replaced when needed.

body.p: A bike with a tidy history is easier to trust, and trust is what turns a hesitant buyer into one who accepts your asking price. A bike with no history raises questions, and buyers tend to answer those questions by offering less.

Receipts get lost and memories blur. A year or two later, you may struggle to say when the chain was last replaced or when the brake fluid was last changed. Recording each job at the time makes it simple to answer, and it makes it simple to show.

body.h: Good records help you ride, too

body.p: A service history is not just for the sale. It is the same information that keeps the bike reliable while you own it. Knowing what was done and when tells you what is coming next, and helps you catch problems earlier.

You do not have to wait for the day you sell. Every service you log today adds to the story. MotoLog keeps your services and mileage in one place on your phone, so when the time comes you have the history ready instead of a drawer of half-remembered receipts.
A well-kept bike is easier to enjoy and easier to sell. The records are how you prove it.

title: Buying a used motorcycle: the checklist to run before you pay
alt: A rider crouching beside a motorcycle in a garage, working on it with a toolkit open beside them
excerpt: A used bike is only a good deal if you know what you are buying. Here is what to ask, check and walk away from.

body.p: Buying used can save you a lot of money, but the price on the advert is only part of the story. What decides whether it is a good deal is how the bike was looked after. This checklist helps you find that out before you hand anything over.

ul: The seller's name matches the registration document.
The frame number on the bike matches the documents.
There is a service history, ideally with dates and mileage.
Any claims about previous owners or accidents are written down, not just promised.

body.p: If a seller cannot or will not show any records, treat that as information. It does not always mean the bike is bad, but it means you are taking their word for it.

Compare the odometer with the service records and the general wear. A low reading with worn pegs, a shiny seat and tired tyres does not add up. A believable history, with mileage rising steadily between services, is far more reassuring than a single round number.

body.h: Look at the bike with the engine cold

ul: Ask the seller not to warm it up before you arrive, so you can hear a cold start.
Look for oil or coolant weeping from the engine, forks and shocks.
Check the chain and sprockets: hooked teeth and a stiff or rusty chain mean money soon.
Read the date code on the tyres. Old rubber hardens even when the tread looks fine.
Squeeze the brake and clutch levers and check they feel smooth and consistent.

body.p: A short test ride tells you more than any photo. Listen for odd noises, notice whether it pulls to one side, and check it shifts cleanly through the gears. If the seller will not allow a ride, ask them why.

Worn tyres, an overdue service or a tired chain are all fair reasons to ask for a lower price, because you will have to pay for them. Point at the specific thing and what it costs, and the conversation stays calm.

Once the bike is yours, the first thing worth doing is writing down the mileage and the date, and then every service from there. It is the same evidence you just asked the seller for. MotoLog keeps your services and mileage in one place on your phone and flags what is due soon or overdue, so you always know where the bike stands.
Buy carefully, and the next owner, whether that is you in five years or someone else, will thank you for the records.

title: How to choose a motorcycle helmet that fits and lasts
alt: A motorcyclist checking their bike and gear before a ride
excerpt: The best helmet is the one that fits your head and gets worn every ride. Here is how to pick one and know when to replace it.

body.p: A helmet is the most important piece of kit you own, and a surprising amount of its protection depends on fit. A good helmet that does not fit is worse than a modest one that does.

Try helmets on in person if you can. It should feel snug all the way round, with the cheek pads firm against your face and no sharp pressure points, especially on your forehead. When you hold the chin bar and try to roll it forwards or sideways, your skin should move with the helmet instead of the helmet sliding over your head.

ul: Wear it for at least ten minutes in the shop. Hot spots show up with time.
Check you can see to the sides without turning the whole helmet.
Fasten the strap and make sure the helmet does not lift off when pulled from the back.

body.h: Look for a recognised safety standard

body.p: Helmets are tested to standards such as ECE 22.06, which is the current European one, or DOT in the United States. The sticker or label shows which one it meets. Check which standard applies where you ride, and be wary of helmets with no labelling at all.

body.h: Pick the style for how you ride

ul: Full face: the most coverage, and the usual choice for fast or long rides.
Modular: the chin bar flips up, handy for commuting and stops.
Open face: lighter and airier, with less protection for your face.
Adventure: a peak and a larger visor opening for mixed roads and trails.

body.p: Replace a helmet after any hard impact, even if it looks fine, because the protective liner may be damaged where you cannot see. Many manufacturers also advise replacing a helmet around five years after you start using it, as materials age. Check what the maker of yours recommends.

Clean the shell and visor with mild soap and water, and avoid strong solvents or stickers that can weaken the shell. Store it somewhere cool and dry and never hang it by its strap on a mirror, where it can get knocked.

It is easy to forget when you bought it. Note the purchase date somewhere you will see it again. If you already keep your rides and bike details in MotoLog, that is a natural place to keep a reminder of how long the helmet has been in use.
Choose well, replace when it is time, and wear it every ride.

title: Five riding skills to practise in an empty car park
alt: A motorcycle on an open road at the start of a journey
excerpt: You do not need a track day to ride better. A quiet car park and an hour is enough to build skills that matter on the road.

body.p: Most of us learn to ride well enough to pass a test and then stop practising. A quiet car park and an hour every few weeks can fix that. Here are five skills worth working on, in the order that usually helps most.

Squeeze the front brake smoothly instead of grabbing it, and add the rear as you slow. Practise from a low speed, building up gradually, until you can stop quickly in a straight line without the bike feeling twitchy. Hard stopping is a habit, so it is worth rehearsing before you ever need it.

Ride in a slow, tight circle using a little rear brake and the clutch friction zone, keeping your head up and looking where you want to go. This is the skill that makes junctions, filtering and parking feel easy.
Look over your shoulder to where you want to finish, keep the revs steady, drag a little rear brake and let the bike lean while you stay upright. Start wide, then slowly tighten the circle.
Set up some cones or markers and practise turning your head to the exit before you turn the bars. The bike follows your eyes. This habit carries straight onto real bends.
Practise rolling the throttle on and off gently and matching your shifts, so the bike never lurches. Smooth riding is safer and easier on the chain, clutch and tyres.

ul: Pick one skill per session instead of trying everything.
Keep sessions short, about an hour, so you stay sharp.
Check your tyre pressures and chain before you go. A quick look takes minutes.
Find a place with no traffic, and ask permission if it is private.

body.p: If you log your rides and mileage in MotoLog, you will see how much you actually ride, and a practice session is a good reason to get out. Mileage between services and trips both build up over a season, and the app keeps them in one place.
Little and often beats one big effort. Your future self on a wet road will be glad you did.

title: Motorcycle service intervals: a plain-English cheat sheet
alt: A motorcycle being serviced in a workshop
excerpt: How often does a motorcycle really need servicing? Typical intervals for common jobs, and why your owner's manual always has the last word.

body.p: Service intervals vary a lot between models, so the single most reliable source is your owner's manual. Think of this guide as a map of what usually gets done and roughly how often, so you know what to look for and what to ask a mechanic about.

Most manufacturers set intervals by whichever comes first: a distance or a time. A bike that only does a few thousand miles a year still needs its oil and fluids changed, because they age even when parked.

ul: Engine oil and filter: often every 3,000 to 8,000 miles, or once a year. Check your manual, as modern engines vary.
Chain: clean and lubricate every few hundred miles and after wet rides, and check the tension regularly.
Tyre pressure: check weekly, and before any long ride.
Brake fluid: commonly every one to two years, because it absorbs moisture over time.
Coolant: usually every two to five years on liquid-cooled bikes.
Air filter: inspect at each service and replace when dirty, often every 6,000 to 12,000 miles.
Spark plugs and valve clearances: set by the manufacturer, and can range from several thousand miles to tens of thousands.
Sport bikes: often tighter intervals, especially for oil and consumables, if ridden hard.
Cruisers: usually relaxed intervals, with the chain or belt checked regularly.
Adventure bikes: dust, mud and weight mean chain, filters and tyres wear faster off the tarmac.
Commuters and scooters: lots of short trips and stop-start riding are hard on oil, so do not stretch intervals.
Off-road bikes: often measured in hours of running time, not miles.

body.h: Do not forget the time limit

body.p: It is easy to track mileage and forget the calendar. Brake fluid, coolant and oil all expire on a date as well as a distance, so a bike that sits in the garage can still be overdue.

Remembering every interval across every part is a lot. MotoLog lets you log each service and set an interval in miles and months, then shows what is due soon or overdue so nothing slips. You enter the numbers from your manual once, and the app does the counting.
Keep to the schedule, keep the records, and your bike will repay you with reliability and a better resale price.
